newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl candidacy lends confidence to economic plans.
newsitem.headline: Kohl candidacy lends confidence to economic plans.

text.p: Helmut Kohl inspired fresh confidence in Germany's drive to join Europe's currency union and overhaul its tax system by vowing on Thursday to stand again as Chancellor next year, economists said.

Kohl, already Germany's longest-serving chancellor, was expected to stand in the 1998 election but eliminated at least some of the uncertainty surrounding his economic policy, saying he planned to see his policies bear fruit.

"Until his statement today, there was some lingering uncertainty about Kohl's reform proposals," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt. "But now things look a little more certain."

Analysts said the near-term implications for financial markets of Kohl's announcement were limited but Kohl might now pursue his policies more vigorously, pushing through reforms favourable for the German stock and bond markets.

But supporters of European economic and monetary union (EMU) have the biggest reason to cheer Kohl's decision, which means that one of the single currency project's strongest backers could see it through a difficult period of preparation.
"It would have been a strong anti-EMU message if Kohl decided not to run," said Gernot Nerb, economist at Salomon Brothers. "He is now almost guaranteed to push forward to meet the EMU criteria."
Economists said Kohl would push for EMU harder than ever as failure of Germany to join the first wave of member nations in 1999 would cripple his reelection chances.
Europe will decide in early 1998 which nations will be allowed to join EMU the following year, based on their economic performances in 1997.
Kohl acknowledged on Thursday that it was extremely difficult to fulfil the economic criteria and timetable for EMU but said he was certain Germany would in the end find a way.
Economists said Kohl's announcement also boosts confidence in plans for tax reform aimed at creating jobs and stimulating the economy with 30 billion marks ($17.9 billion) in tax cuts.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have vigorously opposed aspects of the tax overhaul scheme and economists said they now expected Kohl to push the tax package through.
"He will be taking a higher profile domestically and on the European front," Nerb said.
Economists said the timing of today's announcement was a deft political stroke for the chancellor that could help him win the 1998 general election.
The SPD, which has not yet named its candidate, is widely thought to prefer waiting as long as possible before saying who they will offer to stand against Kohl.

"The SPD now is under pressure to name a candidate this year," said Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber in London. "They would have liked to have been able to wait until regional elections early next year."

She and others said the SPD now had a greater chance of nominating the current SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, who is seen as a weaker opponent to Kohl than alternatives such as Gerhard Schroeder, the SPD premier of Lower Saxony.
"Kohl may now behind in the polls but you should not write him off. He has a knack for coming back," said Rosenstock at IBJ.
